chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
title: Religion in the family and Methodist and Baptist churches
summary: Her family wasn't deeply religious, church-hopped between Baptist and Methodist, and she recalls Salvation Army services.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Was your family very religious?

I wouldn't say that they were. There was a division in the faith. My grandmother on my father's side, they were Methodist and my family on my mother's side were Baptist. So I was a little mixed up I guess. I attended both churches.
You'd go from church to church as you moved around.

Oh, yes. I wasn't too involved in the church. One summer I think I attended a summer program at the Methodist Church, participated in summer activities. But I was quite young then and that's the only time I recall I was really part of the church.

Okay, so your own involvement wasn't that strong.
No, no.
Do you have any recollections, you know, of religious life at that time?
No, I know we had the Baptist Church, we had these --
What would you say was the difference between the Baptist denomination and the Methodist?

And the Methodist? I think that the -- how can I say it -- the church in Homestead, the Baptist Church in Homestead that I knew about, they had a Reverend Morton, I believe his name was, he preached sort of loud and tried to get a lot of converts, I think. The Methodist Church was more settled. They just went about having their services --
Less enthusiasm than the Baptist.
Yeah, I guess it's what the name implies. Well the Methodist Church was above

8th Avenue and the Baptist Church was below 8th Avenue.

That tells us something. Well, I guess, one of the things of interest is how church music connects with other forms of Black music. I was just wondering if you could recall any -- I think Earl Hines for a time played the organ in the church, but not for very long.

Yeah, that's possible. I remember a lot of religious services being held more or less by travelling groups, because they were -- this might have been the Salvation Army because I remember that we used to listen to these services that were held on the corners, you know -- it had to be the Salvation Army.
Those would have been Black churches though.

No. No, they were white. They were mostly white and as I recall they would get on a corner and start and the next thing you know they would have a crowd. It could have been some sort of missionary group, I'm not too sure.
Well, this is the Salvation

Yeah.
How about the Methodist and Baptist?
You know they just had their services at the churches and that was it.
They weren't Black churches.

Oh, yes, they were Black churches, yes, oh, yes. Now, my uncle -- my mother's brother who lived in Ranken, now they were quite church goers, you know. My Uncle Paul, he sang in the choir and Aunt Joe, I guess they practically lived in church most of the time. I remember that -- well, I attended a lot of services at the church where Uncle Paul sang. He sang not only in the choir, but there was a trio that he sang with. That I recall. I suppose that was one of the reasons why he was in church most of the time, rehearsing and being part of the programs there.
